passage:
First week: Farida got into the Hyderabad data-science internship and told everyone it was luck. "They probably mixed up my file." She stayed at the office till ten every night, checking every line of code twice.
Third week: Her mentor praised her dashboard in the team meeting. Farida's face went hot. "Oh, anyone could have done that," she said, and worked straight through lunch. That night she lay awake, sure someone would soon find out.
Fifth week: At the interns' chai break, she finally said it aloud to Nirmala: "I keep thinking I'm a fraud here." Nirmala put her cup down. "Seriously? Me too. Every day." Two others at the table nodded. Farida laughed for the first time in weeks, and that evening she left at six.

qa.q: How late did Farida stay at the office in the first week?
qa.a: She stayed at the office till ten every night.

qa.q: What was Farida afraid of as she lay awake in the third week?
qa.a: She was afraid someone would soon find out she didn't deserve her place.

qa.q: What turning point came in the fifth week, and why did it help?
qa.a: Farida named the feeling aloud to Nirmala and learned that others felt the same, which eased the fear and let her leave at six.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when Farida admitted feeling like a fraud?
qa.a: She seemed relieved to hear it too, since she felt the same every day.

grounding: A capable intern calls her success luck, brushes off praise and overworks, until naming the feeling to peers shows they share it.

passage: Zeenat, sit down. You think your Vidya ma'am was born confident? At twenty-two I joined this very bank as the only woman in the loans section, and I was sure they had hired me by mistake. When the manager praised my report, I said, "Oh, the clerk helped." He hadn't. I came in on Sundays to recheck files nobody had asked me to check. Then one day in the canteen I blurted out to the other new officers, "Do you ever feel you're just pretending?" Mohan, the cleverest of us, went red and said, "Every single day." We laughed so hard the tea spilled. After that, I stopped saying "the clerk helped".

qa.q: Who did Vidya credit when the manager praised the report?
qa.a: Vidya said the clerk had helped, though he hadn't.

qa.q: What was Vidya afraid of when she first joined the bank?
qa.a: She was afraid they had hired her by mistake and that she did not really belong.

qa.q: What turning point helped Vidya stop brushing off praise?
qa.a: She asked the other new officers if they felt they were pretending, and Mohan admitted he felt it every day, which showed her she wasn't alone.

qa.q: How might Mohan have felt when Vidya asked her question in the canteen?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed but relieved, going red before admitting he felt the same.

grounding: A senior colleague recalls feeling like a fraud as a new officer, discounting praise and overworking, until sharing it with peers showed they felt it too.

passage: In the Gurugram architecture office, Suraj spread Sahil's drawings across the table. "The facade is strong. But the stair layout doesn't meet the fire rules. You'll need to redo it." Sahil felt a flicker of heat in his neck. Then he breathed. "You're right. I missed the second exit. That's my mistake." He made a note. "I'm good at facades, not great at the rules yet. Could I sit with Meenal for an hour? She knows them cold." Suraj nodded. "Good idea." Walking back to his desk, Sahil didn't replay the meeting or plan a comeback. He opened the file and started on the stair. At six he left, the stair half-done and the facade still something he was proud of.

"Rukmini, your piece on the flower market was lovely. But you got the vendor's name wrong. He's already called twice."
Rukmini winced, then pulled her notebook closer. "Oh no. Which name?"
"You wrote Gopal. It's Govind."
"That's on me. I copied it from my notes too fast. I'll call him and apologise, and we'll run a correction tomorrow."
"You're taking this well."
"It stings. But one wrong name doesn't make the whole piece bad. The opening's still good, isn't it?"
Divyansh grinned. "The opening's the best thing you've written."
"Then I'll keep that and fix the name. And from now on I'll read names back to people."
"Want me to sit with you while you call?"
"No, I've got it. Thanks, though."

qa.a: Divyansh probably feels relieved and respectful, since honest feedback doesn't make her collapse.

Dear Rashmi-di,
You're the only one I can say this to. When I met Kunal in first year, he told everyone I was the cleverest girl in college. I felt like I was glowing. Now, a year later, I don't recognise myself. If I talk about my day, he talks over me. When he forgot my birthday, somehow I ended up apologising for "making it a big deal". Last week I cried after he called my painting "cute for a beginner", and he said I was too sensitive. I've started believing him. Maybe I am. Is it me?
Can I come home this weekend and talk properly? I think I need someone outside all this to tell me what they see.
Love,
Trisha

passage: Raghav, you asked how I handle Sunil uncle at family weddings. Let your Gautam mama tell you. When I was twenty-two, Sunil and I shared a room in Chennai. Every conversation came back to him: his job, his bike, how everyone else was jealous. If I disagreed, he sulked for days, and I'd end up apologising. One day I just stopped arguing. When he boasted, I'd say, "Good for you," and change the subject. When he asked about my salary, I said, "I'd rather keep that to myself." And when he took my scooter without asking, I said plainly, "Not without asking. That's my rule." He didn't change, beta. I stopped waiting for him to. Forty years on, we still meet at weddings, briefly, and I enjoy the biryani.

qa.a: He stopped arguing for agreement, kept personal things private and stated plain rules, like asking before taking the scooter.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt when Gautam stopped arguing?
